Correspondence

Dear Editor,

In Anne-Marie Sandler's contribution to the “ways of seeing” (J.C.P. Vol. 15 No. 2) she refers to the interesting point I made about “integration, disintegration and reintegration”. What I actually wrote about (see pages 45 to 47) was Dr. Fordham's dynamic of the self described by him as “deintegration and reintegration” which is quite different from disintegration.

Yours sincerely,

James Astor

Dear Editor,

In the Obituary of Jimmy Robertson in the last issue (J.C.P. Vol. 15 No. 2), Mary Boston wrote that Jimmy met me in the Cadbury's factory. In actual fact, it was in the Cadbury's village at Bournville that we met.

We were both students at colleges which were sharing facilities because of the outbreak of war.

For each of us the experience was in great contrast to our working-class backgrounds, and our relationship never lost the shared pleasure in learning.

Yours sincerely,

[[RunningHead]]

“Well, I Couldn't Say No, Could I?”: Difficulties in the Path of Late Adoption**

Frances Salo

Frances Salo

9 Somali Road
London, NW2

Frances Salo  

Mark, when he made the comment above, was referring to the time when he was 10 years old and had been placed with the W. family with a view to adoption. This paper will consider how his underlying wish to “say no” contributed to the initial difficulties in the path of this adoption; it will then go on to consider external factors and the effect which they had, in order to discover something of the tasks and difficulties facing children who are placed for late adoption.

In Britain an active policy of finding homes for older and hard-to-place children has resulted in the placement of large numbers of such children. The Anna Freud Centre's Study Group on Adopted Children has already outlined some of the difficulties which these children experience when facing such a placement, a placement which may from the outside represent the best chance for the child, but which may nevertheless throw his inner life into confusion and upheaval, as earlier feelings of helplessness and anger, fears of rejection, and conflicts about dependency are all reactivated, and certain objects and possibilities are given up and mourned. All these proved complications for Mark in coming to terms with his adoption.

There were other complications specific to Mark's case. His history was one of considerable deprivation: at 2 years 9 months he and two siblings were placed in a children's home when his mother became psychotic, and he remained there until he was 10 years 2 months. He was then placed for adoption with a middle-class white couple who offered a stimulating home environment and were very keen to try and undo the effects of seven years of institutional life so that Mark could be a brother to their son, Ronnie, a black 12-year-old whom they had adopted at birth. Mark's was thus a transracial adoption with all the potential difficulties inherent in such an adoption.

What I think was overlooked when he was placed for adoption was the importance of his relationship with his sister and brother who had been in care with him all along, and from whom he was traumatically separated when each was individually placed. For a long time this stood in the way of his becoming attached to the W's.

[[RunningHead]]

Paediatric Psychotherapy: The Development of a Technique for a Service in a General Paediatric Outpatient Clinic

Susan Dias

Susan Dias

Romford
Essex

Susan Dias  

Donald Winnicott (1958), Anna Freud (1961, 1975), Bergmann and Anna Freud (1965), Isabel Menzies Lyth (1985), the Robertson (1953a, 1953b, 1955, 1958, 1973) and Dora Black (1989) were all pioneers in establishing the importance of the need for communication between paediatricians and child therapists and psychiatrists in the care of paediatric patients. The impact of separation from parents, intrusive medical procedures, chronic illness and bereavement upon the developing child and his or her family have been well documented (Black 1978, Robertson 1953b, 1973, Kashani 1981, Furman 1984, Taylor 1987). For the most part this has been taken into consideration in modern paediatric practice. No ward nowadays forbids access by parents, most nursing care plans try to cater for the emotional well-being of the child, and many consultants attempt to educate their junior medical staff in the importance of appropriate bereavement work.

Historically, medical and nursing training has emphasised interview techniques for how to talk to patients rather than how to listen to the ways in which children and their families communicate their concerns. However, as paediatricians and clinical nurse managers become increasingly aware that a large proportion of their work demands psychological and therapeutic knowledge and skills for which their training does not equip them, child therapists and psychiatrists are called upon to provide appropriate education (Mrazek, 1987, Josse and Challoner, 1987). Predominantly this is done by liaison, consultative work, i.e. attendance at ward rounds and meetings, running staff support groups, and the supervision and formal teaching of medical and nursing staff.

In addition, a crucial factor in the educative process is the treatment of children and their families on an inpatient basis and the communication of aspects of that treatment to relevant medical and nursing staff. This combination of consultative, teaching, and clinical work can lead to the establishment of trust between paediatric and psychological staff, an essential ingredient for any effective holistic approach to paediatric medicine.

[[RunningHead]]

The Eye of the Beholder: Work with a Ten-Year Old Deaf Girl

Elizabeth Urban

Elizabeth Urban

4 Woodchurch Road
London NW6 3PN

Elizabeth Urban  

Introduction

Because the girl I call Virginia is profoundly deaf, eyes and what they see are of paramount importance to her. I think that her material shows that her fantasy of what was in the eye of her beholder was a significant part of her therapy with me. It was this fantasy that changed in the course of our work together, and I hope to explain how this occurred in terms of theory put forward by Michael Fordham.

This work provoked my interest in, and thinking about, the role of the analyst's interest, and of the patient's perception of the nature of that interest. It also brought to my attention the kinds of responses that result from that perception.

By the time Virginia finished her therapy, she seemed to feel that there was a friendly community with which she could communicate and where she might find membership. The deaf community is poorly served by psychiatric services, and only a very few have had the benefit of psychotherapeutic help. It is my hope that this paper will serve to draw attention to this fact, and to stimulate interest in how this situation might be changed.

Background

Virginia came to me for forty-two weekly sessions during her last four terms at primary school. I saw her in my role as social worker at a school for the deaf, and the work we did can best be described as a kind of “psychodynamic play therapy”.

We met in the school medical suite, composed of two small rooms joined by a door. The first room was where I had my desk, telephone, files, and two soft chairs. The second was the medical room, which contained a bed with a screen on wheels around it, a table with chairs, a desk lamp, a sink, a full-length mirror on the back of the door, and miscellaneous medical equipment, including a chart for eye examinations fixed to the wall.

To begin with, there was as much lack of understanding as there was presence of it. Virginia could not speak discernibly, save for a very few words, and although she was being taught signing, she had limited understanding of language and what it was about. I had some signing skills, but the demands of trying to concentrate on what was to me a foreign language (initially poorly expressed by Virginia), of trying to understand what she was trying to communicate of her feelings, and of managing her impulses to run out of the medical suite, often were too much for me to be able to think clearly.

[[RunningHead]]

The Blossom Tree and the Number 4: Some Ideas about Thought Disorder in An Adopted, Diabetic Boy**

Andrea Watson

Andrea Watson

12 Rectory Road
Oxford OX4 1BW

Andrea Watson  

It was during the course of my Infant Observation and supervision with Mrs. Harris that I was introduced to concepts that were of tremendous importance in my work with the boy who is the subject of this paper. One of these, the idea of skin containment, came up many times in our Infant Observation Seminars; the others, from her supervision of a borderline child, are Bion's ideas on thinking and the place of the mother's maternal reverie in creating the conditions necessary for the internalisation of a thinking object.

My patient, Michael, whom I have been seeing in four times a week psychotherapy since January 1984 when he was eleven, is an adopted boy who developed diabetes when he was 4 years 7 months old. He came into therapy with reports of his being “unbearable” both at home and school - a chaotic, argumentative and disruptive boy, prone to outbursts of inappropriate “silly” behaviour, but with no real indications initially as to the depth of his thinking disorder.

Diabetes is an illness whose onset undoubtedly creates the catastrophic change that Bion (1970) talks about, in the sense of an emotional explosion when all previously held views of life are thrown into disarray. One can imagine what the impact of a daily injection of insulin might have on a child's experience of his skin as an adequate - or rather inadequate - container, with all its psychological parallels.

This in itself, therefore, might seem to be enough to explain Michael's difficulties in thinking and learning, but I am going to suggest in this paper that Michael's capacity to think about himself and his relationships both to his internal and external worlds was impaired and well-nigh shattered long before the onset of his diabetes. It is my opinion that it was his removal from his natural mother at six weeks old, followed by pre-adoption fostering before final placement with his adoptive parents, that had the catastrophic effect on his capacity to think that seems amply illustrated in his material. It is not his capacity to make passionate attachments that has been impaired, although much of his energy is, out of fear, spent trying to avoid them because of the dread of having them removed; it is his daring to notice and to think about these attachments, to believe in the willingness of his object to return his affection and remain steadfast, that has been shattered.

[[RunningHead]]

R.D. Hinshelwood. A Dictionary of Kleinian Thought. London: Free Association Books. 1989. £39.95. Revised Paperback Edition 1990, £19.95.

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin  

I approached this book with mixed feelings. This was partly occasioned by the title, which aroused in me some reluctance to accept the confines of the label “Kleinian” just as volumes denoted “Freudian” raise my hackles a little. Not, however, the idea of a dictionary, because Laplanche and Pontalis (1967) was an obvious and excellent reference point, and in any case dictionaries more generally are such delightful source-books. My first readings in it were of the dipping-in variety, and this did not help to settle my doubts, as of course it is easy in such a large volume (500 pages) to find particular entries from which one would diverge or to wonder about omissions. But when I began to look at the book as a whole in a more serious way, I began to appreciate how substantial a contribution it is to the study of those ways of thinking and theorising and doing clinical work which have grown out of Melanie Klein's work. I became very much impressed both by Hinshelwood's immense intellectual energy and by his capacity for lucid exposition, his range of interest, and his overall grasp of both theoretical lines of development and the patterns of psychoanalytic life which have sustained the creative development of Klein's ideas. So when I had given the book the attention it deserves, I felt it was a most useful addition to a personal psychoanalytic library, since the codification and cross-referencing of the dictionary form prove most enlightening.

The book is organised in two parts. Part one consists of thirteen main entries which cover both the major concepts introduced by Klein (paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions, projective identification, etc..) and her revisions of established analytic concepts (e.g. Oedipus Complex, superego, etc.) These are in chronological order in relation to Klein's writings. Hinshelwood says modestly in his introduction that “Possibly these entries could be read as the chapters of an introductory work on Kleinian psychoanalysis” and I think this is a justified statement and that the text will be well used as such an introduction. The method of these entries is to provide a definition, chronology of the main relevant papers and a discursive article, helpfully structured with sub-headings, and ends with a thorough list of references. The labour that Hinshelwood has undertaken will be of enormous benefit to future students from an introductory to an advanced level, because the amount of organised information on each topic is considerable, and the bibliographic sections are a splendid resource.

Elizabeth Young-Bruehl: Anna Freud. A Biography. London: MacMillan. 1989. Price £18.95.

Lydia Tischler

Lydia Tischler

Lydia Tischler  

Anna Freud was born in Vienna in 1895 and died in London on October 9th, 1982, shortly before her 87th birthday. Even though hers was a long life, her achievements would suffice to fill several lifetimes. She had lived through two world wars and in mid-life had to establish herself in a new country.

Her biographer does justice to the many-faceted and complex personality of her subject. She presents a portrait of Anna Freud which is illuminating and which rings true. There is a welcome absence of speculation about Anna Freud's personal life, nor is the reader offered “wild interpretations” about what Anna Freud called “her honourable inner life”. She adheres scrupulously to verifiable sources.

The central theme of this book is Anna Freud's intellectual creativity. The author has tried to tell “how Sigmund and Martha Freud's youngest child, jealous of psychoanalysis, became not only her father's successor and, in her own right, her generation's most scientifically exact and wide-ranging theoretical and clinical contributor, but also a woman whose life was, through and through, psychoanalytic”. Psychoanalysis is also the method the author chooses to describe this “life and work”. Young-Bruehl's formulations are based on the theories about creativity first formulated by Freud and later elaborated by Kris and Greenacre, and these are spelt out in the postscript. In the early formulations, great intellectual creativity was considered to be characterised by virtuosity of day dreaming “in youth and in maturity by an equal admixture of femininity and masculinity and activity and passivity”. Whether the reader will agree with the theoretical formulations concerning the origins of Anna Freud's creativity, her achievements speak for themselves and thankfully Anna Freud's own voice comes through in all its clarity and lucidity in this book.

The story of Anna Freud's life is at the same time the history of psychoanalysis, and she herself considered it to be her twin with which she had to compete for her father's attention. How she resolved this “rivalry” makes fascinating reading. Anna Freud was a private person, fiercely protective of her own and her father's personal privacy. She did not “share the opinion of others that psychoanalysis owes it to the external world to publish this correspondence” (between Freud and Fliess). Her father had often said that he had “revealed enough to the world and the rest was his personal property”. Given her views on this subject, one wonders what she would have made of her own biography. Anna Freud was lucky in her biographer. Young-Bruehl treats her subject with respect and scholarship.

This book is the edited proceedings of a conference organised by the Medical Campaign Against Nuclear Weapons (M.C.A.N.W.) in April 1989. It explores from a variety of angles the reasons (or unreason) for the nuclear arms race. In particular, it questions the motives of the powerful, the so-called objectivity and rationality of the decision processes and reveals the battles for military supremacy, not only between nations but also among the branches of the armed services, air, sea and land.

Dorothy Judd: Give Sorrow Words: working with a dying child. Published by Free Association Books, 1989. £12.95.

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter  

As the duality of the title implies, this book concerns both the highly specialised endeavour of exploring ways to work with a dying child, and also the work, which engages all therapists, of “giving sorrow words”. This is related to the sorrows of loss which accompany all the gains of development and which can prepare the individual for the eventual losses of bereavement and of life itself.

Dorothy Judd is one of the small but increasing number of child psychotherapists who, in recent years, have been applying the insights of psychoanalysis to work with children and adolescents who are physically disabled, chronically ill or, as in this case, terminally ill. Following previous experience of this nature, the writer spent three months regularly visiting Robert, a seven and a half year old, who was in hospital dying of leukaemia. The diary of her times with Robert, her contacts with his parents and the immediate reflections and observations of countertransference which accompany her notes form the central part of the book.

These case notes are preceded and followed by substantial sections which reveal a remarkable depth and breadth of integrative work. Thus we find ourselves not just reading a further example of the extended application of psychoanalytical insights in an exceptionally demanding situation, but rather we feel that we are accompanying the writer in a wide-ranging and deeply reflective process which enhances and enriches these insights. A range of psychoanalytical, psycho-social and medical writings are drawn upon and these gain further significance by illuminations from poetry and art. These studies lead to an increased awareness of the part played by death in the fullness of living, while always retaining the vulnerability of recognising that “what you do not know is the only thing you know” (T.S. Eliot, Four Quartets).

The book also reveals much drawn from the experience of others. Of particular interest are the substantial extracts from interviews with those highly experienced in this field. These include Dr. Dora Black; Margaret Atkin; Dorothy Jordon and Richard Lansdowne of the Great Ormond Street staff and also Mother Frances Dominica who runs a hospice for children.

Otto Weininger: Children's Phantasies. The Shaping of Relationships. Published by Karnac Books, 1989. £14.95.

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson  

In this book Otto Weininger describes his conversations with young children and attempts to illustrate the manifestations of unconscious phantasy as they emerge within the context of very different settings such as playgroups, ordinary and special schools for disturbed children, the family milieu and play therapy. He uses Melanie Klein's theoretical and developmental formulations and explores the relevance of her insights into our work as parents, teachers and clinicians. Weininger himself created, and for eight years directed, a school for emotionally disturbed and educationally underachieving children and many of his examples come from children he helped within this setting. He vividly and convincingly shows how children experience unconscious phantasies as if they are really happening in reality and explains how the reality is altered by such phantasies as revealed by the child's ensuing behaviour.

Editorial

This issue is the first for which a theme was set in advance - work with children with an illness or disability. The response to the call for papers was impressive, revealing how much of this work is being done, and also showing how the setting of a theme prompts people to write and to submit papers that otherwise might not have seen the light of day.

As a result, this journal covers a wide range of work in different settings. It shows how psychotherapists have been learning to adapt their technique and experience to work both with this population of damaged children and with their carers, often without the traditional trappings of psychotherapy.

New ways of working are explored in some of the papers, while in others the setting and method is familiar but the nature of the work and the understanding needed is deeply affected by the special problems facing the patient.

Future issues may again concentrate on a chosen theme. The editorial board would welcome both feedback on this style of journal and suggestions for possible future topics.

Correspondence

Dear Editor,

I am pleased to have been given the opportunity to reply to the review by Asha Phillips of my Video Series “Enriching Day Care”.

The provision of day care for young children is at last being addressed in contemporary economic and political debate, the hidden agenda of which is the value of women and children in society. This issue is not only of importance in this country, but particularly at the moment in Eastern Europe where extremely well-resourced day care is threatened.

I regret therefore that the reviewer seems to have missed the main aim of my videos, which is to try to discuss the question of quality in day care - a part of the debate that gets left out in endless discussions focussing on who should pay and where it should be located. Quality care should enable a real attachment to be made between a child and its carer, though the quality of that relationship varies in different settings, and this has implications for a child's development.

Her conclusion that the three videos should be re-edited into one (presumably “of broadcast quality”) shows her lack of understanding of both the conditions under which the videos were made, and of their different purposes - which, it is true, are not stated overtly.

Firstly, they were never intended to be for a TV audience. Hugo Young's recent article in the Guardian

Andrea Watson  

Introduction

I want, in this paper, to look at a session from the therapy of a little boy, in which he elaborated, in great detail, his theories about the damage that he had caused by his attacks in phantasy, on mummy and inside babies. His anxiety about the power of his phantasised attacks was undoubtedly exacerbated by coincidental external events which I shall mention below.

Martin is a little boy, who came into twice-weekly therapy at the age of 4. The sessions I wish to describe occurred when he had been in therapy for just over six months.

He had had a very troubled early history, but the referral had actually been precipitated by his behaviour during his mother's next pregnancy, although the new baby was a few weeks old by the time he was first seen at the clinic. During the pregnancy he had made violent physical attacks on his mother's body - particularly her tummy. Such behaviour, although worsening during the pregnancy, had been a common occurrence as early as motor control would allow. He had also often appeared to be depressed, this being made manifest in a sad facial expression and moods of great lethargy. There were also dangerous actions which, if not suicidal, were perhaps tempting fate to punish him. For example, he ran out in front of a car, and when rescued by his mother told her that it was his life and if he wanted to kill himself then he would. He also said that if the new baby was a girl he would leave home. The baby was a boy and in fact once he had arrived Martin accepted him quite readily and showed him considerable affection. The temper tantrums and vigorous attempts to control his mother, however, continued virtually unabated.

Early History

The facts of his own early history are of some significance. His mother had an eclamptic fit - the result of toxemia of pregnancy - which probably started during labour itself. She was heavily sedated for at least two weeks thereafter. Martin screamed from birth and steadfastly refused to take the breast. This developed later into a refusal to accept food cooked by his mother. (His very poor eating and depression were reflected in his appearance when he first came into therapy for he was very thin and looked extremely ill with dark shadows under enormous eyes.) His fear of being contaminated by mother spread at one point to his refusing to allow her to dress him or even to touch his clothes - saying that she could point out what he was to wear but not to touch them or they would have to be washed again. His early screaming led to him being taken into hospital at 4 weeks and his mother being told to leave him to scream.

How exciting that video is entering child psychotherapists’ field of communication! This was my first thought when asked to review these three videos.

I was immediately faced with the question of how to view them: as an ordinary member of a television audience, as an interested student of the subject matter with pen and paper at hand or as a reviewer with my remote control at the ready to replay passages at will? I tried to keep all of these in mind.

The three videos explore different day care settings and their effects upon the young children attending them. Two of the films look at particular centres and one is a comparative study of different styles of day care.

I shall look at the general study first.

Enriching Day Care

This film is presented like an illustrated lecture, with headings written out on the screen. Five different sorts of day care are considered, with particular focus on individual children in some cases. The settings covered are a private day nursery, a family centre (Buddle Lane), a child minder at home, a nursery school (the Anna Freud Nursery), and a playgroup. The main headings are enlightening in themselves as to what is important in Day Care. They are:

Facilitating secure attachments and dealing with separation in a day care setting.

Managing transitions in day care.

Appropriate working practices in day care.

Assessment, observation and discussion.

Joint work with parents.

Support for staff.

Jill Hodges  

This is a paper about adopted children's representations of the self and of objects, and how these representations are related to each other and to experience. The sources of this paper are varied; one is the psychoanalytic research done at the Anna Freud Centre in the Study Group on Adopted Children begun under Maria Berger's chairmanship, and these psychoanalytic data will be the main focus here. A second source is research I carried out in a study initiated by Professor Barbara Tizard. This examined children who spent their earliest years in residential nurseries before eventual adoption or restoration to their biological parents. Consideration of this will take us somewhat into recent developments in “attachment theory”. A third source has been the writings of other workers.

This is therefore a hybrid paper, and it presents something of an elephant-and-whale problem. The elephant, as the largest terrestrial mammal, and the whale, as the largest aquatic one, might well have interesting things to say to each other about their respective experiences. But is very difficult for them to get into any kind of communication, precisely because the one is terrestrial and the other is aquatic. This paper attempts to set up some kind of a dialogue.

Let me start by outlining something of the research findings from the study of children who spent their early years in residential institutions. This study was begun almost twenty years ago, by Barbara Tizard, as a study of the development of two-year-olds who had been cared for in residential nurseries since four months of age or earlier (Tizard & Tizard, 1971). These two-year-olds were compared with others who had always lived in intact families in their own homes. Subsequently, more children were added to the study, and followed up at the age of four-and-a-half. Let us pause at this point and look at what issues are relevant for us here.

Bowlby, in 1951, characterized maternal deprivation as “not uncommonly almost complete in institutions… where the child often has no one person who cares for him in a personal way and with whom he feels secure”. Such, it seems, was the environment of the “nursery” children. The residential nurseries provided good physical care and play facilities for the children, who were cared for in groups of six. They were generously staffed; but mainly bcause they functioned as training institutions for child-care staff, there was very little continuity of care.

Coping Processes in Well-Adjusted Chronically Ill Patients on a Paediatric Ward**

Pauline Cohen

Pauline Cohen

4 Kidderpore Gardens
London NW3 7SR

Pauline Cohen  

Introduction

Many young patients with serious organic disease or chronic physical illness develop a remarkable capacity to cope with their illness, especially when one considers that each has his or her own life experiences and developmental struggles, apart from the ongoing trauma of the illness. Anna Freud (1952) alerts one to the fact that unconscious fears and fantasies are aroused by the experience of illness and its treatment and that children react excessively to pain when latent unconscious fantasies are dominant.

The medical and nursing team on the ward where I worked dealt skilfully with the children when their ability to cope lapsed. Many young patients, who had been known to the paediatric team for many years, were encouraged by the staff to spend short periods on the ward when the symptoms of their condition appeared to be exacerbated during periods of stress or crisis. Only in unusual circumstances were child psychotherapists asked to intervene. A good relationship between the paediatric and child psychiatry team was a necessary condition for successful intervention.

Three vignettes will be presented. They demonstrate the challenging task confronting a child psychotherapist when regressive or self-destructive behaviour is unremitting and becomes an interference with medical treatment and the healing process.

The aim of the interventions was to restore the capacity of the patient to cope and thereby to facilitate the role of the nurses as primary caretakers.

Case Material: Peter

Peter, aged 19, had been a patient on the paediatric ward for the previous three years. He had generalised histiocytosis and was admitted regularly for treatment. He suffered with recurrent back and leg pains and had Harrington rods inserted to relieve his back pain. The disease shifted to various organs and he required major lung surgery. He remained under the care of the hospital surgeons and physicians.

Peter was very knowledgeable about his illness, dealing with this entirely on his own and admitting himself to the ward when necessary.

Raddlebarn Road

Linda Winkley  

Introduction

Questions about the quality of life have become increasingly relevant for all staff who work with children suffering from chronic illness. As well as the psychological and social problems associated with chronic illness, for children with chronic renal failure there are the additional problems of adjusting to dialysis and transplantation and the anxieties associated with these procedures. As a consultant to the unit I saw my role as working with the team towards improving the adjustment and quality of life for the children. Over time it gradually became clear that the most effective way of helping facilitate the normal processes of growth and development in the children was through discussion and consultation with the staff.

To put the work into context it is useful to have some understanding of the setting. The renal unit is a small one-storey building set in the grounds of a large district general hospital which provides the only haemodialysis facilities for children and adolescents from infancy to 17 years for a very large geographical area. Dr. N., consultant paediatric nephrologist, devoted much of his personal time and energy to raising the money to build the unit. It comprises one moderately sized dialysis room to accommodate four children with a small kitchen and a very small secretary's room leading off it. Usually there is an atmosphere of activity and work in the unit, with a sense of vitality conveyed by the cheerfulness of the nurses and teacher. Informality is encouraged with staff and parents using first names and it does feel like a family at times, with the mothers helping with other children and making drinks for everyone. However, the warmth and out-goingness of the staff contrasts with the isolation of the children; they sit far apart and rarely talk to one another whilst on dialysis. This emotional withdrawal is well recognized as occurring with both adults and children and will be discussed in more detail later on.

As an institution, therefore, the renal unit forms only a very small part of the larger institution of the hospital. There is no doubt that the institutional task is first and foremost to keep the children alive. However, I do feel there is a secondary task which is to work for the children's emotional well being. Clearly the first task has to take priority, but there is an awareness of the team working to improve the quality of life for the children and this very much takes into account their emotional and social adjustment.

Freud was always interested in psychiatry. In fact, he was on the whole quite happy to use the then current psychiatric classification of mental illnesses, and saw psychoanalysis as a treatment method within that wider discipline. Since his time the major developments in both psychoanalytic thinking and the increasing sophistication of psychiatric classification has led to a wide divergence of thinking between the two. Such is the current situation that it is often difficult to relate the concepts of one to those of the other, and some would think that this is a loss to both. In particular psychoanalytic thinking has found it increasingly difficult to find an acceptable nosology. Gone are the once frequent diagnoses of hysterical or obsessional neurotic states. Now cases tend to be formulated around a core conflict described in terms of the diagnostician's particular theoretical orientation. This move away from classification may be inevitable, but what tends to be lost is any specificity about the severity and psychopathology of the case.

All the authors of this book are psychoanalysts with wide experience in psychiatry and one of their purposes is to re-establish the connection between the psychiatric conceptualisation of mental illness and the developmental perspective that is based on classical psychoanalytic concepts. Of particular interest are the chapters on psychotic conditions and a group brought together by the authors under the heading of “Non-neurotic developmental disorders”. The latter is a rather mixed bag of disturbances of varying severity that are neither psychotic, nor primarily due to conflict and compromise formation. What they have in common, in the author's view, is that they have an early developmental deficit due to either environmental or constitutional causes.

Introduction

In writing about a child's early life, ideally one hopes to construct a coherent narrative about their earliest history. Jack's history, however, is one of discontinuity. It is fractured through a series of abrupt separations, changes of caretaker and losses. There are, too, many gaps and absences in our knowledge of the quality of care he received in various hands. It is hardly surprising that with these frequent early ruptures, one of the referring symptoms should have been his “muddles”.

Jack was the result of a casual liaison between Mrs. G, a 42-year-old alcoholic woman, and a man who lived in the same building. At the time of Jack's conception, Mrs. G's husband would have been in prison. Apart from the name, nothing is known about the biological father who disappeared when Jack was 6 months old. Jack's “stepfather” (Mrs. G's husband) came out of prison just before Jack's birth and assumed full responsibility for the child.

The marriage was unstable and at the time of referral had long since ended. The stepfather (possibly unbeknownst to Jack) had a new relationship and child, whilst Jack's mother, having successfully overcome her alcoholism for the past five years, was working and living quietly on her own in Edinburgh.

Nothing was directly known about the quality of care Jack had received in his early life. However, there would have been frequent heavy drinking bouts interspersed with marital disputes. When Jack was 5 months old his mother was arrested for being drunk. As she was unable to care for Jack, he had the first of what was to be a long line of brief separations from her. By the age of two he had had eight brief receptions into Care and two “social stays” in hospital. When Jack was 18 months old, concern at his parents’ inability to provide consistent care led to his name being placed on the “At Risk” register. One could surmise that whilst there may, sporadically, have been an adequate “holding environment” there would also have been periods of neglect and possible exposure to frightening adult behaviour.

Narcissistic Organisations and Sexual Identity—A Clinical Presentation

Margaret Cohen

Margaret Cohen

Margaret Cohen  

Introduction

If we believe that children's development and sexual identification depends on the object relations they have achieved, then we must consider what happens where this achievement has not truly taken place. We are aware that in some cases a child turns away from relying or is unable to rely on an internal object, and sets up an internal structure of its own from which it hopes to gain protection and security.

This “turning away” has been seen in a variety of ways by different psycho-analysts. For instance: Mrs Klein described vividly the role played by envy, and this has been developed by Kleinians into a theory of narcissistic organisation. Guntrip talked more in terms of fear and intolerable vulnerability. More recently Meltzer has developed the Kleinian picture and talked about the aesthetic conflict - the overpowering aesthetic impact of the mother on the baby, and his conflicts around the inaccessibility of her internal world, that is, around her essential mysteriousness. To this list we certainly have to add the failure of the external object to give the child a basis for object relatedness - so that the turning away would be reactive.

Whichever view of the causation one takes, and I do not intend to explore this in depth here, there is a turning away from the object to an internal narcissistic structure - that is, to a manufactured object - an object of one's own making. Of course, the character of the turning away will affect the nature of the narcissistic structure, and the content of the work needing to be done in therapy. But I consider that there are some characteristics which are common to narcissistic states:

The suppression of vulnerable infantile needs - this involves a cruel attitude to the infantile part of the personality;

The manufacture of an invulnerable, supposedly protective, big-brother part of the personality, which is frequently clever at propagandising against vulnerability and object relatedness;

Suspicion of an object that tries to get in touch with the needy part as this is seen as jeopardising the defensive structure.

The Importance of Beauty in the Psychoanalytic Experience**

Susan Reid

Susan Reid

15 Pandora Road
London NW6 1TS

Susan Reid  

“If ever any beauty I did see Which I desir'd and got, twas but a dreame of thee”

(John Donne: “The good-morrow”)

In this paper I set out to describe how a very young boy, two years and one month when he commenced therapy, whom I shall call Georgie, who, on beginning therapy seemed more animal than human, discovered beauty, and having done so, an appetite for life which he had just about decided was not worth the living. In the last section of the paper I set out to discuss the idea that beauty and its linked attributes goodness, hope and truth, form the bedrock for mental health in all of us.

But to begin at the beginning: I would like to start by giving some background history.

Background History

Georgie was born to a white mother, Ann, following a brief relationship with an Afro-Caribbean man. Georgie has never known his father and it is unlikely that his father knows of his existence.

Ann is said to have started having difficulties when she was thirteen: she became quiet and withdrawn and her scholastic performance suffered. She was put on probation when sixteen years old for shoplifting and spent some time in a hostel. She left home to take up a job in London and a number of casual jobs followed. In the subsequent years there was little contact between Ann and her family.

Ann became pregnant and a daughter was born, also the result of a brief relationship with an Afro-Caribbean man. This daughter died at eight weeks, a cot death, and Ann blamed nursing staff. At this time Ann's mental illness became apparent: she was paranoid and hallucinating.

When Ann became pregnant again, this time with Georgie, she sought no ante-natal care and delivered the baby herself at home. When a few days old, Georgie was admitted to hospital with breathing difficulties, and as a result of her disturbed behaviour Ann was admitted to hospital under Section 2 of the Mental Health Act. Ann appealed against the Section and was regraded as an informal patient. Whilst it was recommended that she should not be allowed to leave with Georgie and that a care order should be made, this did not happen.

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry

Garden Flat
15 Lambolle Road
London, NW3

Anne Hurry  

Introduction

Kevin was 19 when referred to a Consultation Centre because of his self-cutting. He had no awareness of his motivation for cutting, and little capacity for self-observation. He spent much of his initial interviews complaining of physical symptoms, blaming others for his difficulties and fearing others would see him as homosexual. Chronologically in late adolescence, he had found no acceptable sexual identity. His masculinity, his femininity and his homosexuality were all intolerable to him. Unable to remain the dependent child or be the little girl he longed to be (or felt he was) he switched repeatedly from one identification to another. Gratification of his sexual fantasies had to be avoided as too bad, too dangerous to himself or others. Most of all he condemned his paedophilic fantasies about little girls. His sexuality and his aggression were channelled into self-destructive acting out: drinking, burning himself with cigarettes, cutting his face and stomach, getting himself attacked, and attempting suicide by throwing himself down the underground stairs. His experience of affect was often short-circuited via somatisation, in giddy fits, pains, and, at times, epileptic fits.

In current literature there is considerable agreement that the roots of difficulties in gender identification and sexual perversion lie in the pre-oedipal phase, although they may be reinforced in the oedipal phase and at later stages. Many authors describe difficulties in the separation-individuation phase (Mahler, 1965) as fundamental, resulting in the lack of a fully differentiated sense of self, and an ongoing longing for and terror of merging. (See for instance, Blum, 1977; Karasu and Socarides, 1979; Rosen, 1979). Some authors, notably Socarides, (1979b) and Volkan (1979) have pointed to the rapprochement sub-phases as critical. A number of writers point to the unintegrated, shifting and apparently superficial quality of the identifications in severe cases. (Glasser [1985a] suggests that such identification be termed “simulations” since true identifications are not possible for these patients with their intense fear of annihilation).

Psychotherapy with Hospitalized Children with Leukaemia: Is it Possible?

Ricky Emanuel , Anita Colloms , Annette Mendelsohn , Helen Muller and Rita Testa

Rita Testa

Pond Street
London NW3

Rita Testa  

Introduction

The prognosis for Childhood Leukaemia has changed considerably in recent years. In the past, this constellation of diseases was inevitably fatal whereas with the progress made in medical research particularly with new forms of chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation, the cure rate (meaning the complete eradication of the physical symptoms of the disease for over 5 years) for leukaemia can now be as high as 60 to 70%. Children are required to have usually 3 or 4 courses of intravenous chemotherapy. After each course, they are required to spend approximately a month in protective isolation being barrier nursed in sterile conditions until their immune systems recover enough to allow them to have safe exposure to everyday life. If the chemotherapy is successful in bringing about a remission of the disease, it has been found that a bone marrow transplant can be highly effective in some forms of leukaemia in curing the disease. Preferably a matched donor is found (usually a sibling) and healthy bone marrow is transfused into the leukaemic child. This process in itself is not too traumatic, however prior to this the child has to undergo several extensive tests including bone marrow aspirations and lumbar punctures. They also require other prophylactic treatments including total body radiation. These treatments invariably render the children infertile as well as making them feel very ill. Temporary hair loss always occurs. A further period of time in isolation is required after transplant before the child can be cared for in out-patients. A close check is kept on the children for many years necessitating frequent hospital visits and tests. So although the child's life may be saved, the treatment of leukaemia is highly invasive and is potentially psychologically scarring. We will be discussing children who have been treated with both conventional chemotherapy as well as those who have undergone bone marrow transplantation.

There is a large body of literature on the psychological aspects of childhood cancer which is well reviewed by Van Dongen-Melman and Sanders-Woudstra (1986). They consider the main stressors on the child following diagnosis and the treatment period to be: the life threatening nature of the disease; the physical discomfort; the bodily changes; the requirement for hospitalisation involving long periods in protective isolation and follow up outpatient care. Koocher and O'Malley (1981) remark on the anxiety present in the remission period where there is the feeling of ever-present doom mixed with hope in the child and parents.

Joan Raphael-Leff  

Shortly after I had completed an infant-observation course while training, I myself had a baby, and squirmed as I looked back on the reasonable detached reports I had written about an intimate situation observed from the outside. The lesson was one I retained when supervising baby observations myself at the Institute of Psychoanalysis. I am, therefore, delighted to find in this book not only descriptive material drawn from weekly observation-reports of trainees but, in the commentary on these, some attempt to gain an internal focus - access to emotional events subjectively lived inside the family, observed and experienced through the observer's countertransference. Although commendably sparing in its aim not to ‘over-direct’ the reader, the interpretive discussion following each fragment of observation treats the narrative as a text to be read creatively. It tries to extract from the observation the meanings implicit in the powerfully charged unfolding process of emotional reformulation following the birth of a baby. This commentary is thus similar to a secondary process of elaboration on case-material such as occurs during group discussions in infant observation training seminars, while leaving the original text intact and open to inspection for the reader to draw his or her own conclusions.
